_comment: 🛑🛑 DO NOT APPLY THIS FILE YET. 🛑🛑
S3 bucket policy ADDITION — agrisync-raw-ap-south-1. Denies the two
actions that could turn 178-objects-recoverable-today into gone-forever:
s3:DeleteObjectVersion (permanently erases a noncurrent version, no
undelete) and s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration (a lifecycle rule that expires
noncurrent versions achieves the same permanent loss on a delay — this is
the 'lifecycle rule applied in error' scenario named in the backup task).
spec: raw-bucket-backup-recovery (dispatched task, no plan-doc §N yet)
runbook: _COFOUNDER/runbooks/raw-bucket-backup-recovery.md
WHY THIS IS PHASE 2, NOT SAFE TO APPLY TODAY: both Deny statements below
carry a StringNotLike escape for one named role, agrisync-raw-breakglass-
role. THAT ROLE DOES NOT EXIST YET. Applying this policy before the role
exists denies these two actions to EVERYONE, including the root account —
not a hazard today (nobody legitimately calls DeleteObjectVersion or
PutLifecycleConfiguration on this bucket as part of normal operation) but
there needs to be a working escape hatch in place before this locks, or
the next time this bucket genuinely needs a lifecycle change (e.g. to
raise the backup's Object Lock retention, or to add a rule this bucket
itself may eventually need) someone has to talk their way past a policy
with no valid principal at all.
REQUIRED BEFORE APPLYING:
1. Create agrisync-raw-breakglass-role: an IAM role that (a) only a
human principal can assume (not an instance profile / not the app
role), and (b) requires MFA to assume, via a trust-policy condition
Bool: {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}. This mirrors the
shape of aws/raw/replication-role-trust-policy.json's principal-
scoping discipline but trusts a human IAM principal instead of the
S3 service.
2. Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> below with the real account ID (951921970996 in
the account this was authored against — do not hardcode it in this
committed file; apply-config.sh should substitute it the same way
apply-replication.sh substitutes the replication role ARN).
3. Merge the two statements below into bucket-policy.json's Statement
array (do not apply as a second separate put-bucket-policy call —
that replaces the whole document and would silently drop the
existing DenyInsecureTransport statement). Apply via
aws/raw/apply-config.sh as one transaction, matching the CMK deny
rail's own instruction on this point.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER — stated plainly, not glossed over:
- It does not stop someone who can call iam:PutRolePolicy /
sts:AssumeRole against the breakglass role itself from then deleting
versions freely. A bucket policy can restrict WHICH principal may act,
but cannot stop an account admin from first granting themselves that
principal's identity. This raises the bar (requires a second,
deliberate, loggable IAM action first) — it does not make deletion
impossible. Only Object Lock in Compliance mode does that, and only
for the bucket it is set on (the backup, not this source bucket,
since Object Lock cannot be added to an existing bucket at all — see
create-backup-bucket.sh's header comment).
- It does not stop s3:DeleteBucketPolicy — an account admin can always
remove this policy entirely and then delete versions freely. This is
a bucket-policy-shaped tool, not an IAM-boundary-shaped one; it stops
accidents and casual/scripted mistakes (the stated threat: 'a
lifecycle rule applied in error'), not a determined or compromised
root/admin credential. Credential compromise at the admin level is
covered by the CROSS-REGION BACKUP existing at all, not by this file —
see the runbook's coverage-comparison table.
- It does not touch s3:DeleteObject (creating a NEW delete marker on a
still-current object) — that action is left alone deliberately.
Soft-delete-via-marker is recoverable (it is exactly the mechanism
that made the 178 recoverable) and is not the hazard this rail exists
to close; DELETING THE MARKER'S OWN VERSION, or the object's other
noncurrent versions, is s3:DeleteObjectVersion — which this DOES deny.
D9 note: DenyPutLifecycleConfigurationExceptBreakglass does not itself add
or remove any lifecycle action — it restricts WHO may change the
lifecycle document, which today (per lifecycle-policy.json) contains no
expiring actions at all. No D9 conflict.
